questions.prompt: Explain what size classes are in 2 to 5 sentences. List the horizontal size classes for iPhone portrait and full-screen iPad.

rubric.criterion: Explains that size classes abstract screen space into compact and regular categories
Identifies compact horizontal for iPhone portrait and regular horizontal for full-screen iPad

questions.modelAnswer: Size classes abstract device screen dimensions into two semantic categories: compact and regular. A compact size class indicates constrained space, while a regular size class indicates expansive space. An iPhone in portrait orientation provides a compact horizontal size class, whereas an iPad running full screen provides a regular horizontal size class.

questions.prompt: Explain how NavigationSplitView in SwiftUI adapts across different screen sizes and multitasking modes in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that NavigationSplitView renders side-by-side columns on regular width
Explains that it automatically collapses into a single navigation stack on compact width

questions.modelAnswer: In SwiftUI, NavigationSplitView provides multi-column navigation that automatically adapts to the active size class. When horizontal space is regular, such as on full-screen iPad, it renders sidebar, content, and detail columns side-by-side. When the window shrinks to compact width in Split View or on iPhone, it automatically collapses those columns into a single navigation stack.

questions.prompt: Explain why checking UIDevice.current.userInterfaceIdiom is an anti-pattern when building adaptive layouts in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that an iPad running in Slide Over or Split View has compact width identical to an iPhone
Explains that checking device idiom forces wide tablet layouts into narrow windows, causing clipping

questions.modelAnswer: Checking UIDevice userInterfaceIdiom is an anti-pattern because hardware does not dictate available window space. On an iPad, users can run an app in Slide Over or Split View. This assigns the window a compact width identical to an iPhone. Forcing wide tablet layouts into narrow windows causes clipped text and broken views.

questions.prompt: Explain why UIScreen.main.bounds is deprecated in modern iOS and what developers should use instead in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that UIScreen.main reflects physical screen dimensions rather than multitasking window size
Explains using view bounds, container geometry, or GeometryReader to determine available layout space

questions.modelAnswer: Apple deprecated UIScreen.main.bounds due to iPad multitasking features like Split View and Stage Manager. In these modes, the app window occupies only a portion of the display. Querying physical screen bounds gives an inaccurate measurement that exceeds the active viewport. Instead, developers should inspect view bounds, container geometry, or use SwiftUI GeometryReader.

questions.prompt: Explain how a senior iOS engineer architects an app to support Stage Manager and freeform window resizing in 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

rubric.criterion: Discusses relying on fluid Auto Layout constraints, adaptive size classes, and ViewThatFits rather than fixed frames
Discusses registering for trait changes with modern registerForTraitChanges and supporting multi-scene sessions

questions.modelAnswer: A senior engineer treats the app window as an arbitrary, dynamically resizable viewport rather than a fixed screen. They construct view hierarchies using fluid Auto Layout constraints and adaptive containers like ViewThatFits and NavigationSplitView. In UIKit, they observe updates using registerForTraitChanges, and in Info.plist they configure multiple scene support with UISceneConfiguration for concurrent multitasking sessions.
